claim: FBF-1 restricts the rate of meiotic entry in C. elegans germline stem cells.
source: We find that two PUF family RNA-binding proteins FBF-1 and FBF-2 have opposite effects on Caenorhabditis elegans germline stem cell dynamics: FBF-1 restricts the rate of meiotic entry, while FBF-2 promotes both cell division and meiotic entry rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing meiotic entry rates in different genetic backgrounds (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).

claim: FBF-2 promotes both cell division and meiotic entry rates in C. elegans germline stem cells.
source: We find that two PUF family RNA-binding proteins FBF-1 and FBF-2 have opposite effects on Caenorhabditis elegans germline stem cell dynamics: FBF-1 restricts the rate of meiotic entry, while FBF-2 promotes both cell division and meiotic entry rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing cell division rates (Figure 1E) and meiotic entry rates (Figure 1F) in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: FBF-1-mediated post-transcriptional control requires the activity of CCR4-NOT deadenylase.
source: Antagonistic effects of FBFs are mediated by their distinct activities toward the shared set of target mRNAs, where FBF-1-mediated post-transcriptional control requires the activity of CCR4-NOT deadenylase, while FBF-2 is deadenylase-independent and might protect the targets from deadenylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments showing that CCR4-NOT is required for FBF-1 function (Figure 3B, Figure 3C,D).

claim: FBF-2 is deadenylase-independent and might protect target mRNAs from deadenylation.
source: Antagonistic effects of FBFs are mediated by their distinct activities toward the shared set of target mRNAs, where FBF-1-mediated post-transcriptional control requires the activity of CCR4-NOT deadenylase, while FBF-2 is deadenylase-independent and might protect the targets from deadenylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by poly(A) tail length analysis showing that FBF-2 protects targets from deadenylation (Figure 5) and CCR4-NOT knockdown experiments showing FBF-2 function is independent of CCR4-NOT (Figure 3B).

claim: The regulatory differences between FBF-1 and FBF-2 depend on protein sequences outside of the conserved PUF family RNA-binding domain.
source: These regulatory differences depend on protein sequences outside of the conserved PUF family RNA-binding domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with chimeric FBF proteins showing that variable regions outside the RNA-binding domain determine functional differences (Figure 6, Figure 7).

claim: The opposing FBF-1 and FBF-2 activities serve to modulate stem cell division rate simultaneously with the rate of meiotic entry.
source: We propose that the opposing FBF-1 and FBF-2 activities serve to modulate stem cell division rate simultaneously with the rate of meiotic entry.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations showing coordinated changes in cell division and meiotic entry rates in fbf mutants (Figure 1D-F) and the ability to uncouple these processes by disrupting regulation of specific targets (Figure 2).

claim: The C. elegans hermaphrodite germline is maintained by about 200-250 mitotically dividing stem and progenitor cells at the distal end of the gonad.
source: It is maintained by a stem cell niche that supports about 200–250 mitotically dividing stem and progenitor cells at the distal end of the gonad (collectively called SPCs, Figure 1A,Bii).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is consistent with the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A single somatic distal tip cell serves as a stem cell niche and activates the GLP-1/Notch signaling necessary for SPC pool maintenance.
source: A single somatic distal tip cell serves as a stem cell niche and activates the GLP-1/Notch signaling necessary for SPC pool maintenance (Austin and Kimble, 1987), which in turn supports germline development (Hansen and Schedl, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Austin and Kimble, 1987; Hansen and Schedl, 2013).

claim: Mitotic divisions of SPCs are not oriented in C. elegans germline.
source: Mitotic divisions of SPCs are not oriented and there doesn't appear to be a correlation between the position of cell divisions distributed throughout the SPC zone and the position of cells undergoing meiotic entry at the proximal end of the zone (Crittenden et al., 2006; Fox et al., 2011; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Maciejowski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Crittenden et al., 2006; Fox et al., 2011; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Maciejowski et al., 2006).

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-1(ok91) is approximately 15 germ cell diameters.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Lamont et al., 2004), we observed that the SPC zone of fbf-1(ok91, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~15 germ cell diameters, gcd; Figure 1Bi) is smaller than that of the wild type (~20 gcd, Figure 1Bii), whereas the SPC zone of fbf-2(q738, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~25 gcd, Figure 1Biii) is larger than that of the wild type (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The SPC zone of wild type C. elegans is approximately 20 germ cell diameters.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Lamont et al., 2004), we observed that the SPC zone of fbf-1(ok91, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~15 germ cell diameters, gcd; Figure 1Bi) is smaller than that of the wild type (~20 gcd, Figure 1Bii), whereas the SPC zone of fbf-2(q738, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~25 gcd, Figure 1Biii) is larger than that of the wild type (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-2(q738) is approximately 25 germ cell diameters.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Lamont et al., 2004), we observed that the SPC zone of fbf-1(ok91, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~15 germ cell diameters, gcd; Figure 1Bi) is smaller than that of the wild type (~20 gcd, Figure 1Bii), whereas the SPC zone of fbf-2(q738, loss-of-function mutation, lf) (~25 gcd, Figure 1Biii) is larger than that of the wild type (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct measurements shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The mitotic index of fbf-1(lf) is 54% higher than that of the wild type.
source: We found that the mitotic index of fbf-1(lf) was significantly higher than that of the wild type (by 54%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mitotic index of fbf-2(lf) is 42% lower than that of the wild type.
source: By contrast, the mitotic index of fbf-2(lf) was significantly lower than that of the wild type (by 42%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The median G2 length of fbf-2(lf) is 25% greater than that of the wild type.
source: We found that the median G2 length of fbf-2(lf) is significantly greater than that of the wild type, suggesting that loss of FBF-2 results in slower progression through the G2-phase of the cell cycle (by 25%; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The median G2 length of fbf-1(lf) is not significantly different from that of the wild type.
source: By contrast, the median G2 length of fbf-1(lf) is not significantly different from that of the wild type (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FBF-2 accelerates SPC cell cycle by facilitating the G2-phase progression.
source: We conclude that FBF-2 accelerates SPC cell cycle by facilitating the G2-phase progression.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that fbf-2(lf) has a longer G2 phase (Figure 1D) and slower cell division rate (Figure 1E).

claim: fbf-2(lf) significantly increased SPC doubling time from 6.1 hr to 8.1 hr.
source: Exponential fits revealed that fbf-2(lf) significantly increased SPC doubling time from 6.1 hr to 8.1 hr (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of larval germ cell proliferation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: fbf-1(lf) does not affect the rate of germ cell division.
source: By contrast, there was no significant difference in germ cell proliferation rate between fbf-1(lf) and the wild type.
evidence: The claim is supported by larval germ cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: fbf-1(lf) results in a 31% increased rate of meiotic entry compared to the wild type.
source: We found that fbf-1(lf) results in a significantly increased rate of meiotic entry compared to the wild type (by 31%; Figure 1F), whereas fbf-2(lf) results in a significantly reduced rate of meiotic entry (by 18%; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on meiotic entry rates shown in Figure 1F.

claim: fbf-2(lf) results in an 18% reduced rate of meiotic entry compared to the wild type.
source: We found that fbf-1(lf) results in a significantly increased rate of meiotic entry compared to the wild type (by 31%; Figure 1F), whereas fbf-2(lf) results in a significantly reduced rate of meiotic entry (by 18%; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on meiotic entry rates shown in Figure 1F.

claim: fbf-2(lf) enhances the overproliferative phenotype of glp-1(ar202) at 15°C.
source: We found that fbf-2(lf) is a strong enhancer of glp-1(gf) since 97% fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) animals have tumorous germlines with 24% germlines showing complete tumors, even at the permissive temperature of 15°C (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1 showing germline phenotypes at 15°C.

claim: 97% of fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) animals have tumorous germlines at 15°C.
source: We found that fbf-2(lf) is a strong enhancer of glp-1(gf) since 97% fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) animals have tumorous germlines with 24% germlines showing complete tumors, even at the permissive temperature of 15°C (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: 24% of fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) germlines show complete tumors at 15°C.
source: We found that fbf-2(lf) is a strong enhancer of glp-1(gf) since 97% fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) animals have tumorous germlines with 24% germlines showing complete tumors, even at the permissive temperature of 15°C (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Four cyclin B family genes provide overlapping as well as specific mitotic functions in C. elegans.
source: Four cyclin B family genes provide overlapping as well as specific mitotic functions in C. elegans (van der Voet et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (van der Voet et al., 2009).

claim: cyb-2.1 mRNA is found in complex with FBFs across multiple experimental conditions.
source: Since cyb-2.1 mRNA is found in complex with FBFs across multiple experimental conditions and contains more canonical FBE sites in its 3'UTR than the other cyclin B transcripts, we selected cyb-2.1 for further analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on prior experimental data from Porter et al., 2019 and Prasad et al., 2016 as cited in the manuscript.

claim: cyb-2.1 contains more canonical FBE sites in its 3'UTR than the other cyclin B transcripts.
source: Since cyb-2.1 mRNA is found in complex with FBFs across multiple experimental conditions and contains more canonical FBE sites in its 3'UTR than the other cyclin B transcripts, we selected cyb-2.1 for further analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of cyclin B 3'UTRs.

claim: Steady-state transcript levels of 3xflag::cyb-2.1(fbm) are approximately 4.5 fold greater than those of 3xflag::cyb-2.1(wt).
source: Quantification of transgene transcript levels by qPCR suggested that steady-state transcript levels of 3xflag::cyb-2.1(fbm) were ~4.5 fold greater than those of 3xflag::cyb-2.1(wt), suggesting that FBEs affect steady-state transcript levels (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of 3xFLAG::CYB-2.1 protein is increased approximately 1.4 fold in 3xflag::cyb-2.1(fbm) animals compared to 3xflag::cyb-2.1(wt).
source: By immunoblotting, we found that the expression of 3xFLAG::CYB-2.1 protein was increased ~1.4 fold in 3xflag::cyb-2.1(fbm) animals compared to 3xflag::cyb-2.1(wt), suggesting that the presence of FBEs decreases protein production from cyb-2.1 mRNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of FBEs decreases protein production from cyb-2.1 mRNA.
source: By immunoblotting, we found that the expression of 3xFLAG::CYB-2.1 protein was increased ~1.4 fold in 3xflag::cyb-2.1(fbm) animals compared to 3xflag::cyb-2.1(wt), suggesting that the presence of FBEs decreases protein production from cyb-2.1 mRNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of protein levels between constructs with wild-type and mutated FBEs (Figure 2C).

claim: C. elegans SPCs express five PUF-family proteins that cluster into three groups based on sequence similarity: FBF-1/–2, PUF-8, and PUF-3/–11.
source: C. elegans SPCs express five PUF-family proteins that cluster into three groups based on sequence similarity: FBF-1/–2, PUF-8, and PUF-3/–11 (Ariz et al., 2009; Crittenden et al., 2002; Haupt et al., 2020; Lamont et al., 2004; Stumpf et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies (Ariz et al., 2009; Crittenden et al., 2002; Haupt et al., 2020; Lamont et al., 2004; Stumpf et al., 2008).

claim: Each of the three PUF groups has a distinct RNA-binding specificity.
source: Each of the three PUF groups has a distinct RNA-binding specificity (Bernstein et al., 2005; Koh et al., 2009; Opperman et al., 2005), so it is likely that FBEs in cyb-2.1 3'UTR are predominantly recognized and regulated by FBFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bernstein et al., 2005; Koh et al., 2009; Opperman et al., 2005).

claim: The SPC doubling time of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm is significantly shorter than that of fbf-2(lf).
source: We found that the SPC doubling time of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm was significantly shorter than that of fbf-2(lf) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on germ cell doubling time shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is no significant difference in the doubling time between fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1wt and fbf-2(lf).
source: By contrast, there was no significant difference in the doubling time between fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1wt and fbf-2(lf) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on germ cell doubling time shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is no significant difference in SPC meiotic entry among fbf-2(lf), fbf-2(lf); cyb-2.1wt, and fbf-2(lf); cyb-2.1(fbm).
source: Indeed, there was no significant difference in SPC meiotic entry among fbf-2(lf), fbf-2(lf); cyb-2.1wt, and fbf-2(lf); cyb-2.1(fbm) (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by meiotic entry rate data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm is approximately 32 germ cell diameters.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm (~32 gcd, Figure 2Fiii) is significantly larger than that of the fbf-2(lf) (~26 gcd, Figure 2Fi, G, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-2(lf) is approximately 26 germ cell diameters.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm (~32 gcd, Figure 2Fiii) is significantly larger than that of the fbf-2(lf) (~26 gcd, Figure 2Fi, G, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: There is no significant difference in the length of SPC zone between the fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1wt and fbf-2(lf).
source: By contrast, there is no significant difference in the length of SPC zone between the fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1wt and fbf-2(lf) (Figure 2Fii, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm after cyb-2.1(RNAi) is approximately 26 germ cell diameters.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm after cyb-2.1(RNAi) became significantly shorter (~26 gcd) compared to the control RNAi (~31 gcd; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm after control RNAi is approximately 31 germ cell diameters.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); 3xflag::cyb-2.1fbm after cyb-2.1(RNAi) became significantly shorter (~26 gcd) compared to the control RNAi (~31 gcd; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CCR4-NOT deadenylase is a complex that includes three core subunits: two catalytic subunits CCR-4/CNOT6/6L and CCF-1/CNOT-7/8 and a scaffold subunit LET-711/CNOT1.
source: CCR4-NOT deadenylase is a complex that includes three core subunits: two catalytic subunits CCR-4/CNOT6/6L and CCF-1/CNOT-7/8 and a scaffold subunit LET-711/CNOT1, which are highly conserved in C. elegans and humans (Figure 3A; Nousch et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Nousch et al., 2013) and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: CCR4-NOT RNAi dramatically shortened the SPC zone in fbf-2(lf) compared to the control RNAi.
source: First, we measured the extent of SPC zone after RNAi-mediated knockdown of core CCR4-NOT subunits, and found that CCR4-NOT RNAi dramatically shortened the SPC zone in fbf-2(lf) compared to the control RNAi (p<0.01; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lengths of SPC zones in the wild type and fbf-1(lf) animals are not significantly affected by CCR4-NOT knockdown.
source: By contrast, the lengths of SPC zones in the wild type and fbf-1(lf) animals were not significantly affected by CCR4-NOT knockdown (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CCR4-NOT is required for FBF-1-mediated regulation of germline SPC zone length.
source: Our findings suggest that CCR4-NOT is required for FBF-1-mediated regulation of germline SPC zone length, but does not significantly contribute to FBF-2 function.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that CCR4-NOT knockdown affects SPC zone length in fbf-2(lf) but not in fbf-1(lf) or wild type (Figure 3B).

claim: CCR4-NOT does not significantly contribute to FBF-2 function.
source: Our findings suggest that CCR4-NOT is required for FBF-1-mediated regulation of germline SPC zone length, but does not significantly contribute to FBF-2 function.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that CCR4-NOT knockdown affects SPC zone length in fbf-2(lf) but not in fbf-1(lf) or wild type (Figure 3B).

claim: Derepression of GFP::H2B::htp-2 3'UTR reporter was observed in 63-69% germlines of rrf-1(lf); fbf-2(lf) genetic background after CCR4-NOT RNAi.
source: We observed derepression of the reporter in SPCs of 63–69% germlines of rrf-1(lf); fbf-2(lf) genetic background (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on reporter derepression shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Derepression of GFP::H2B::htp-2 3'UTR reporter was observed only in 3-5% of rrf-1(lf) and rrf-1(lf); fbf-1(lf) genetic backgrounds after CCR4-NOT RNAi.
source: By contrast, derepression of the reporter was observed only in 3–5% of rrf-1(lf) and rrf-1(lf); fbf-1(lf) genetic backgrounds (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data on reporter derepression shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex is necessary for FBF-1-mediated repression of target mRNAs in germline SPCs.
source: These data suggest that the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex is necessary for FBF-1-mediated repression of target mRNAs in germline SPCs, but is dispensable for FBF-2 regulatory function.
evidence: The claim is based on reporter derepression experiments (Figure 3C,D) and SPC zone length measurements after CCR4-NOT knockdown (Figure 3B).

claim: CCR4-NOT is dispensable for FBF-2 regulatory function.
source: These data suggest that the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex is necessary for FBF-1-mediated repression of target mRNAs in germline SPCs, but is dispensable for FBF-2 regulatory function.
evidence: The claim is based on reporter derepression experiments (Figure 3C,D) and SPC zone length measurements after CCR4-NOT knockdown (Figure 3B).

claim: FBF-1 protein abundance does not decrease after CCF-1 knockdown compared to the control.
source: We found that FBF-1 protein abundance does not decrease after CCF-1 knockdown compared to the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: FBF-1 localization is not affected by CCF-1 knockdown.
source: Immunostaining for the endogenous FBF-1 showed that in control germlines FBF-1 localized in foci adjacent to perinuclear P granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) as previously reported (Voronina et al., 2012). Upon CCF-1 knockdown, FBF-1 foci were still observed next to P granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: CCR4-NOT is not required for FBF-1 expression and localization.
source: Therefore, we conclude that CCR4-NOT is not required for FBF-1 expression and localization, and CCR4-NOT knockdown specifically disrupts FBF-1 function.
evidence: The claim is based on immunoblot and immunostaining data showing FBF-1 levels and localization are maintained after CCF-1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F).

claim: Both endogenous FBF-1 and GFP::FBF-1 foci colocalize with 3xFLAG::CCF-1 foci in SPC cytoplasm.
source: Using co-immunostaining of endogenous FBF-1 or GFP::FBF-1 and 3xFLAG::CCF-1 followed by Pearson's correlation coefficient analysis based on Costes' automatic threshold (Costes et al., 2004), we found that both endogenous FBF-1 and GFP::FBF-1 foci colocalize with 3xFLAG::CCF-1 foci in SPC cytoplasm (Figure 4A,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4A,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The colocalization between GFP::FBF-2 and 3xFLAG::CCF-1 is significantly less robust than that between FBF-1 and CCF-1.
source: By contrast, the colocalization between GFP::FBF-2 and 3xFLAG::CCF-1 is significantly less robust (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Proximity ligation assay detected significantly more dense PLA signals in 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-1 than in the control.
source: We observed significantly more dense PLA signals in 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-1 than in the control (Figure 4D; p<0.0001, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: PLA foci density in mitotic germ cells of 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-2 is not different from the control.
source: By contrast, PLA foci density in mitotic germ cells of 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-2 was not different from the control (Figure 4D; Table 2), although the expression of GFP::FBFs or GFP alone in mitotic germ cells appeared similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4D and Table 2.

claim: FBF-1 colocalizes with CCR4-NOT in SPCs.
source: Together, these data suggest that FBF-1, but not FBF-2, colocalizes with CCR4-NOT in SPCs, in agreement with the dependence of FBF-1 function on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on colocalization and PLA data (Figure 4).

claim: FBF-2 does not colocalize with CCR4-NOT in SPCs.
source: Together, these data suggest that FBF-1, but not FBF-2, colocalizes with CCR4-NOT in SPCs, in agreement with the dependence of FBF-1 function on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on colocalization and PLA data (Figure 4).

claim: The poly(A) tail distributions of cyb-2.1 and htp-1 mRNAs in fbf-2(lf) are both shifted to shorter lengths compared to the wild type background.
source: PAT-PCR assays using RNA samples extracted from fbf-1(lf); glp-1(gf), glp-1(gf), and fbf-2(lf); glp-1(gf) revealed that the poly(A) tail distributions of cyb-2.1 and htp-1 mRNAs in fbf-2(lf) were both shifted to shorter lengths compared to the wild type background (Figure 5A,B,D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A,B,D,E.

claim: In fbf-1(lf) background, the poly(A) tail profiles of cyb-2.1 and htp-1 mRNAs are shifted to longer lengths.
source: Conversely, in fbf-1(lf) background, the poly(A) tail profiles of cyb-2.1 and htp-1 mRNAs were shifted to longer lengths (Figure 5A,B,D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A,B,D,E.

claim: The poly(A) tail of the control unc-54 mRNA does not decrease in fbf-2(lf) background or increase in fbf-1(lf) compared to the wild type.
source: By contrast, the poly(A) tail of the control unc-54 mRNA did not decrease in fbf-2(lf) background or increase in fbf-1(lf) compared to the wild type (Figure 5C,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C,F.

claim: FBF-1 promotes deadenylation of FBF target mRNAs.
source: We conclude that FBF-1 promotes deadenylation of FBF target mRNAs and FBF-2 protects the targets from deadenylation.
evidence: The claim is based on PAT-PCR data showing longer poly(A) tails in fbf-1(lf) (Figure 5).

claim: FBF-2 protects target mRNAs from deadenylation.
source: We conclude that FBF-1 promotes deadenylation of FBF target mRNAs and FBF-2 protects the targets from deadenylation.
evidence: The claim is based on PAT-PCR data showing shorter poly(A) tails in fbf-2(lf) (Figure 5).

claim: The steady-state abundance of FBF targets in fbf-2(lf) decreased relative to the wild type.
source: The steady-state abundance of FBF targets in fbf-2(lf) decreased relative to the wild type and the decrease was significant for all transcripts except him-3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of most FBF targets in the fbf-1(lf) are not significantly different from those in the wild-type background, except for cyb-2.1.
source: The levels of most FBF targets in the fbf-1(lf) were not significantly different from those in the wild-type background, except for cyb-2.1 that accumulated to significantly lower levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The abundance of unc-54 mRNA does not decrease in either fbf-1(lf) or fbf-2(lf) genetic backgrounds.
source: By contrast, the abundance of unc-54 mRNA did not decrease in either genetic background.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Shorter poly(A) tails of FBF targets in fbf-2(lf) are associated with lower mRNA accumulation for many targets.
source: We conclude that shorter poly(A) tails of FBF targets in fbf-2(lf) are associated with lower mRNA accumulation for many targets.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between PAT-PCR data (Figure 5) and qPCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: FBF-1 and FBF-2 share 89% identity in their protein sequences.
source: Despite 89% identity between FBF-1 and FBF-2 protein sequences, several reports suggest that FBF-1 and FBF-2 localize to distinct cytoplasmic RNA granules and have unique effects on the germline SPC pool (Lamont et al., 2004; Voronina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison and is supported by citations to prior research (Lamont et al., 2004; Voronina et al., 2012).

claim: The SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-2(vrm) is significantly longer than that maintained by GFP::FBF-2(wt) and the endogenous FBF-2.
source: We found that the SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-2(vrm) (Figure 6Biv) is significantly longer than that maintained by GFP::FBF-2(wt) (Figure 6Biii) and the endogenous FBF-2 (p<0.01; Figure 6Bi, C) suggesting that the GFP::FBF-2(vrm) effect on SPC zone length is distinct from that of FBF-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Expression of GFP::FBF-2(vrm) is comparable to that of GFP::FBF-2(wt).
source: Western blot analysis indicated that expression of GFP::FBF-2(vrm) is comparable to that of GFP::FBF-2(wt), so their distinct effects on SPC zone length are likely due to functional differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP::FBF-2(vrm) does not rescue fbf-2(lf).
source: Interestingly, we found that the extent of SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) is similar to that of fbf-2(lf) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that GFP::FBF-2(vrm) does not rescue fbf-2(lf).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP::FBF-2(vrm) rescues fbf-1(lf).
source: By contrast, the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) is significantly longer than that of fbf-1(lf) (p<0.01, Figure 6D) and there is no significant difference in the SPC zone length between fbf-1(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) and the wild type, suggesting that the GFP::FBF-2(vrm) rescues fbf-1(lf).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The three VRs outside of FBF-2 RNA-binding domain (VR1, 2, and 4) are important for FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of germline SPC zone.
source: We conclude that the three VRs outside of FBF-2 RNA-binding domain (VR1, 2, and 4) are important for FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of germline SPC zone and mutation or deletion of these VRs resulted in a mutant protein FBF-2(vrm) that functions similar to FBF-1.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments showing that FBF-2(vrm) rescues fbf-1(lf) but not fbf-2(lf) (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Mutation or deletion of VRs 1, 2, and 4 resulted in a mutant protein FBF-2(vrm) that functions similar to FBF-1.
source: We conclude that the three VRs outside of FBF-2 RNA-binding domain (VR1, 2, and 4) are important for FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of germline SPC zone and mutation or deletion of these VRs resulted in a mutant protein FBF-2(vrm) that functions similar to FBF-1.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments showing that FBF-2(vrm) rescues fbf-1(lf) but not fbf-2(lf) (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits becomes significantly shorter than the control.
source: We found that SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits becomes significantly shorter than the control (p<0.01, Figure 6E), suggesting that GFP::FBF-2(vrm) function requires CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 6E.

claim: GFP::FBF-2(vrm) function requires CCR4-NOT.
source: We found that SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-2(vrm) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits becomes significantly shorter than the control (p<0.01, Figure 6E), suggesting that GFP::FBF-2(vrm) function requires CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on the effect of CCR4-NOT knockdown on SPC zone length in the FBF-2(vrm) background (Figure 6E).

claim: PLA foci density in the mitotic cells of 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-2(vrm) is significantly greater than in the control.
source: Furthermore, if GFP::FBF-2(vrm) cooperates with CCR4-NOT, we expect that it might associate with CCF-1 by proximity ligation assay. Indeed, PLA foci density in the mitotic cells of 3xflag::ccf-1; gfp::fbf-2(vrm) was significantly greater than in the control (Figure 6F; Table 3; p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 6F and Table 3.

claim: The VRs outside of FBF-2 RNA-binding domain are required for FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of SPC zone and to prevent FBF-2 from cooperating with CCR4-NOT.
source: We conclude that the VRs outside of FBF-2 RNA-binding domain are required for FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of SPC zone and to prevent FBF-2 from cooperating with CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on experiments showing that FBF-2(vrm) functions like FBF-1 and requires CCR4-NOT (Figure 6E,F).

claim: The SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) is significantly shorter than that maintained by GFP::FBF-1(wt) and endogenous FBF-1.
source: SPC zone length assessment showed that the SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) (Figure 7Biii) is significantly shorter than that maintained by GFP::FBF-1(wt) (Figure 7Bv) and endogenous FBF-1 (p<0.0001; Figure 7Bii, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: The SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) is similar to that maintained by the GFP::FBF-1(wt).
source: By contrast, the SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) (Figure 7Biv) is similar to that maintained by the GFP::FBF-1(wt) (Figure 7Biv, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) functions similarly to FBF-2.
source: This finding suggested that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) might function similarly to FBF-2.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that the SPC zone maintained by GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) is shorter than wild-type FBF-1, similar to FBF-2 (Figure 7B,C).

claim: The protein expression levels of GFP::FBF-1, GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3), and GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) are comparable.
source: Western blot analysis revealed that the protein expression levels of GFP::FBF-1, GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3), and GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) were comparable, so the differential effects on SPC zone length are likely due to functional differences (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) does not rescue fbf-1(lf).
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr4) is similar to that of fbf-1(lf) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) does not rescue fbf-1(lf).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) rescues fbf-2(lf).
source: Interestingly, SPC zone of fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr4) is significantly shorter than that of fbf-2(lf) (p<0.01, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) rescues fbf-2(lf).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) rescues fbf-1(lf), but not fbf-2(lf).
source: By contrast, GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) rescues fbf-1(lf), but not fbf-2(lf) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The presence of VR4 from FBF-2 in a chimeric GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) protein is sufficient to impart FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of SPC zone.
source: We conclude that the presence of VR4 from FBF-2 in a chimeric GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) protein is sufficient to impart FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of SPC zone.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments showing that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) rescues fbf-2(lf) but not fbf-1(lf) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr4) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits is similar to the control.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr4) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits is similar to the control (Figure 7D), suggesting that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) function in SPCs does not rely on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) function in SPCs does not rely on CCR4-NOT.
source: We found that the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr4) after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits is similar to the control (Figure 7D), suggesting that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) function in SPCs does not rely on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of effect of CCR4-NOT knockdown on SPC zone length in the FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) background (Figure 7D).

claim: The SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr3) is significantly shortened after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits compared to the control.
source: By contrast, the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr3) is significantly shortened after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits compared to the control (p<0.01, Figure 7D), indicating that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) maintains dependence on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is supported by SPC zone length measurements after RNAi shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) maintains dependence on CCR4-NOT.
source: By contrast, the SPC zone of fbf-1(lf) fbf-2(lf); gfp::fbf-1(fbf-2vr3) is significantly shortened after RNAi of CCR4-NOT subunits compared to the control (p<0.01, Figure 7D), indicating that GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) maintains dependence on CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on the effect of CCR4-NOT knockdown on SPC zone length in the FBF-1(FBF-2vr3) background (Figure 7D).

claim: FBF-2 VR4 in a chimeric GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) protein is sufficient to support FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of germline SPC zone and to prevent the chimera's cooperation with CCR4-NOT.
source: We conclude that FBF-2 VR4 in a chimeric GFP::FBF-1(FBF-2vr4) protein is sufficient to support FBF-2-specific effect on the extent of germline SPC zone and to prevent the chimera's cooperation with CCR4-NOT.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments and CCR4-NOT knockdown experiments showing that VR4 is sufficient to confer FBF-2-like function (Figure 7).

claim: C. elegans germline SPC cell cycle is characterized by a very short G1 phase.
source: One characteristic feature of C. elegans germline SPC cell cycle is a very short G1 phase (Fox et al., 2011; Furuta et al., 2018), reminiscent of the short G1 phase observed in mammalian embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Becker et al., 2006; Kareta et al., 2015; White and Dalton, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fox et al., 2011; Furuta et al., 2018).

claim: Mouse and human ESCs maintain robust cell division rates supported by a cell cycle with a short G1 phase.
source: Mouse and human ESCs maintain robust cell division rates supported by a cell cycle with a short G1 phase, while the length of S and G2 phases is similar to that observed in differentiated somatic cells (Becker et al., 2006; Chao et al., 2019; Kareta et al., 2015; Stead et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Becker et al., 2006; Chao et al., 2019; Kareta et al., 2015; Stead et al., 2002).

claim: C. elegans SPCs retain G2 checkpoints despite the shortened G1 phase.
source: Similarly, C. elegans SPCs retain G2 checkpoints despite the shortened G1 phase (Butuči et al., 2015; Garcia-Muse and Boulton, 2005; Lawrence et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Butuči et al., 2015; Garcia-Muse and Boulton, 2005; Lawrence et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2009).

claim: Germ cells and ESCs are characterized by a shortened G1 phase and maintain a constitutive robust expression of G1/S regulators Cyclin E and CDK2 throughout the cell cycle.
source: Unlike somatic cells' G1 phase that is triggered and marked by increased amounts of cyclins E and D (Aleem et al., 2005; Guevara et al., 1999), germ cells and ESCs are characterized by a shortened G1 phase and maintain a constitutive robust expression of G1/S regulators Cyclin E and CDK2 throughout the cell cycle (Fox et al., 2011; Furuta et al., 2018; White and Dalton, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fox et al., 2011; Furuta et al., 2018; White and Dalton, 2005).

claim: PUF proteins are expressed in germ cells of many animals and are conserved regulators of stem cells.
source: PUF proteins are expressed in germ cells of many animals and are conserved regulators of stem cells (Salvetti, 2005; Wickens et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Salvetti, 2005; Wickens et al., 2002).

claim: FBF-1 and FBF-2 share the majority of their target mRNAs.
source: C. elegans PUF proteins expressed in germline SPCs, FBF-1 and FBF-2, share the majority of their target mRNAs (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016) and are redundantly required for SPC maintenance (Crittenden et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016).

claim: FBF-1 and FBF-2 are redundantly required for SPC maintenance.
source: C. elegans PUF proteins expressed in germline SPCs, FBF-1 and FBF-2, share the majority of their target mRNAs (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016) and are redundantly required for SPC maintenance (Crittenden et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Crittenden et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 1997).

claim: FBF-1 and FBF-2 localize to distinct cytoplasmic RNA granules.
source: Despite 89% identity between FBF-1 and FBF-2 protein sequences, several reports suggest that FBF-1 and FBF-2 localize to distinct cytoplasmic RNA granules and have unique effects on the germline SPC pool (Lamont et al., 2004; Voronina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lamont et al., 2004; Voronina et al., 2012).

claim: FBF-1 and FBF-2 each support distinct numbers of SPCs.
source: FBF-1 and FBF-2 each support distinct numbers of SPCs (Lamont et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Lamont et al., 2004).

claim: FBF-1 inhibits accumulation of target mRNAs in SPCs, while FBF-2 primarily represses translation of the target mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, FBF-1 inhibits accumulation of target mRNAs in SPCs, while FBF-2 primarily represses translation of the target mRNAs (Voronina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Voronina et al., 2012).

claim: DLC-1 is a cofactor specific to FBF-2 that promotes FBF-2 localization and function.
source: Some differences between FBF-1 and FBF-2 function might be explained by their association with distinct protein cofactors, as we previously found that a small protein DLC-1 is a cofactor specific to FBF-2 that promotes FBF-2 localization and function (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Wang et al., 2016).

claim: FBFs repress their target mRNAs by binding to the FBF-binding elements (FBEs; UGUxxxAU) in the 3'UTRs.
source: FBFs repress their target mRNAs by binding to the FBF-binding elements (FBEs; UGUxxxAU) in the 3'UTRs (Bernstein et al., 2005; Crittenden et al., 2002; Merritt and Seydoux, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bernstein et al., 2005; Crittenden et al., 2002; Merritt and Seydoux, 2010).

claim: Four mRNAs encoding Cyclin B family members co-purify with FBF proteins.
source: Four mRNAs encoding Cyclin B family members co-purify with FBF proteins and three of them contain predicted FBEs in their 3'UTRs (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016).

claim: Three of the four cyclin B family mRNAs contain predicted FBEs in their 3'UTRs.
source: Four mRNAs encoding Cyclin B family members co-purify with FBF proteins and three of them contain predicted FBEs in their 3'UTRs (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016).

claim: Measuring the extent of progenitor zone by counting the number of cell rows positive for mitotic marker REC-8 provides a reliable estimate of progenitor cell numbers.
source: Measuring the extent of progenitor zone by counting the number of cell rows positive for mitotic marker REC-8 provides a reliable estimate of progenitor cell numbers and correlates with progenitor cell numbers in the key genotypes including wild type, fbf-1(lf), and fbf-2(lf) (R2 = 0.779; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SYGL-1 and LST-1 are key transcriptional targets of GLP-1/NOTCH that promote germline stem cell fate.
source: Previous research identified SYGL-1 and LST-1 as key transcriptional targets of GLP-1/NOTCH that promote germline stem cell fate (Kershner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Kershner et al., 2014).

claim: SYGL-1 and LST-1 are cofactors of both FBFs that promote FBF-dependent regulation.
source: SYGL-1 and LST-1 are cofactors of both FBFs that promote FBF-dependent regulation (Haupt et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Haupt et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2017).

claim: The abundance of SYGL-1 and LST-1 impacts the number of uncommitted stem cells and thus the overall size of SPC zone.
source: The abundance of SYGL-1 and LST-1 impacts the number of uncommitted stem cells and thus the overall size of SPC zone (Haupt et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Haupt et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2017).

claim: Both SYGL-1 and LST-1 are FBF targets.
source: Remarkably, both SYGL-1 and LST-1 are also FBF targets (Kershner and Kimble, 2010; Kershner et al., 2014; Prasad et al., 2016), and it would be interesting to investigate whether changes in SPC zone length in fbf mutants are associated with altered levels or pattern of expression of SYGL-1 and/or LST-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kershner and Kimble, 2010; Kershner et al., 2014; Prasad et al., 2016).

claim: Slower accumulation of the FBF target GLD-1 has been documented in fbf-2(lf) background.
source: Slow meiotic entry rate in fbf-2(lf) likely results from enhanced translational repression of FBF targets that regulate differentiation; indeed, slower accumulation of the FBF target GLD-1 has been documented in this genetic background (Brenner and Schedl, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Brenner and Schedl, 2016).

claim: Mutations of FBF targets gld-2 and gld-3 lead to a decrease in meiotic entry rate and to accumulation of excessive numbers of SPCs.
source: In a similar fashion, mutations of FBF targets gld-2 and gld-3 lead to a decrease in meiotic entry rate and to accumulation of excessive numbers of SPCs (Eckmann et al., 2004; Fox and Schedl, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Eckmann et al., 2004; Fox and Schedl, 2015).

claim: FBF-2 represses FBF target transcripts in fbf-1(lf) background, while sequestering them in large cytoplasmic aggregates.
source: FBF-2 represses FBF target transcripts in fbf-1(lf) background, while sequestering them in large cytoplasmic aggregates (Voronina et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Voronina et al., 2012).

claim: Partial derepression of GLD-1 has been observed in fbf-1(lf).
source: However, this repression is less effective than that exerted by FBF-1 since partial derepression of GLD-1 has been previously observed in fbf-1(lf) (Brenner and Schedl, 2016; Crittenden et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Brenner and Schedl, 2016; Crittenden et al., 2002).

claim: The proximal SPC zone contains non-cycling cells in meiotic S-phase, estimated to comprise 30-40% of total SPC zone cells in the wild-type germlines.
source: The proximal SPC zone contains non-cycling cells in meiotic S-phase, estimated to comprise 30–40% of total SPC zone cells in the wild-type germlines (Crittenden et al., 2006; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Fox et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Crittenden et al., 2006; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Fox et al., 2011).

claim: FBFs recognize the same FBE 3'UTR motif and bind largely same mRNAs.
source: In vitro and in vivo studies have revealed that FBFs recognize the same FBE 3'UTR motif and bind largely same mRNAs (Bernstein et al., 2005; Prasad et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Bernstein et al., 2005; Prasad et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2019).

claim: CYB-3 has emerged as a major G2 regulator in C. elegans germline stem cells.
source: Among the B-type cyclins, CYB-3 has emerged as a major G2 regulator in C. elegans germline stem cells (Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Lara-Gonzalez et al., 2019).

claim: cyb-3 lacks canonical FBE elements in its 3'UTR.
source: Since cyb-3 lacks canonical FBE elements in its 3'UTR, testing whether FBFs might regulate CYB-3 levels to control SPC division rate will require identification of the relevant non-canonical binding sites.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of cyb-3 3'UTR.

claim: Deadenylation contributes to PUF-mediated translational repression.
source: Multiple studies suggest that deadenylation contributes to PUF-mediated translational repression (Goldstrohm et al., 2006; Kadyrova et al., 2007; Van Etten et al., 2012; Weidmann et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Goldstrohm et al., 2006; Kadyrova et al., 2007; Van Etten et al., 2012; Weidmann et al., 2014).

claim: CCR4-NOT deadenylation machinery is conserved in evolution from yeast to humans.
source: CCR4-NOT deadenylation machinery is conserved in evolution from yeast to humans (Collart et al., 2017; Wahle and Winkler, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Collart et al., 2017; Wahle and Winkler, 2013).

claim: Deadenylation is required for germline stem cell maintenance in flies, nematodes and mice.
source: Although deadenylation is required for germline stem cell maintenance in flies, nematodes and mice (Berthet et al., 2004; Fu et al., 2015; Joly et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2004; Nousch et al., 2019; Shan et al., 2017; Suh et al., 2009), the contribution of deadenylation to PUF translational repression in vivo is still controversial (Weidmann et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Berthet et al., 2004; Fu et al., 2015; Joly et al., 2013; Nakamura et al., 2004; Nousch et al., 2019; Shan et al., 2017; Suh et al., 2009).

claim: Previous studies of CCR4-NOT component CCF-1 in C. elegans suggested that paralogous PUF proteins FBF-1 and FBF-2 might employ both CCF-1-dependent and CCF-1-independent regulatory modes.
source: Previous studies of CCR4-NOT component CCF-1 in C. elegans suggested that paralogous PUF proteins FBF-1 and FBF-2 might employ both CCF-1-dependent and CCF-1-independent regulatory modes (Suh et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Suh et al., 2009).

claim: PUF RNA-binding domain is sufficient for a direct interaction with the CCF-1 subunit of CCR4-NOT and its homologs in multiple species, including C. elegans.
source: PUF RNA-binding domain is sufficient for a direct interaction with the CCF-1 subunit of CCR4-NOT and its homologs in multiple species, including C. elegans (Goldstrohm et al., 2006; Hook et al., 2007; Kadyrova et al., 2007; Suh et al., 2009; Van Etten et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Goldstrohm et al., 2006; Hook et al., 2007; Kadyrova et al., 2007; Suh et al., 2009; Van Etten et al., 2012).

claim: Protein sequences outside of the well-structured RNA-binding domain can promote PUF-induced deadenylation.
source: However, protein sequences outside of the well-structured RNA-binding domain can promote PUF-induced deadenylation and are hypothesized to function either through improved recruitment of CCR4-NOT complex or through allosteric activation of CCR4-NOT (Webster et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Webster et al., 2019).

claim: Human, mouse, and C. elegans PUF proteins repress Cip/Kip family cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors.
source: Human, mouse, and C. elegans PUF proteins repress Cip/Kip family cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (Kalchhauser et al., 2011; Kedde et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kalchhauser et al., 2011; Kedde et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019).

claim: Repression of Cip/Kip family cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors by PUF proteins is important for cell cycle progression of human and mouse cells through G1.
source: This repression was found to be important for cell cycle progression of human and mouse cells through G1 (Kedde et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kedde et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2019).

claim: Mitotic cyclins B and A are among the core targets of PUF proteins across species.
source: Additionally, mitotic cyclins B and A are among the core targets of PUF proteins across species including nematode FBFs (Kershner and Kimble, 2010; Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016), Drosophila Pumilio (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999), human and mouse PUM1 and PUM2 (Chen et al., 2012; Galgano et al., 2008; Hafner et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2008), and yeast Puf proteins (Gerber et al., 2004; Wilinski et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research across multiple species (Kershner and Kimble, 2010; Porter et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2016; Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2012; Galgano et al., 2008; Hafner et al., 2010; Morris et al., 2008; Gerber et al., 2004; Wilinski et al., 2015).

claim: Cyclin B regulation by PUFs contributes to cell cycle control of Drosophila embryonic cell divisions.
source: Cyclin B regulation by PUFs contributes to cell cycle control of Drosophila embryonic cell divisions (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999; Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007) and to the control of meiotic resumption during Xenopus and zebrafish oocyte maturation (Kotani et al., 2013; Nakahata et al., 2003; Ota et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999; Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007).

claim: Cyclin B regulation by PUFs contributes to the control of meiotic resumption during Xenopus and zebrafish oocyte maturation.
source: Cyclin B regulation by PUFs contributes to cell cycle control of Drosophila embryonic cell divisions (Asaoka-Taguchi et al., 1999; Vardy and Orr-Weaver, 2007) and to the control of meiotic resumption during Xenopus and zebrafish oocyte maturation (Kotani et al., 2013; Nakahata et al., 2003; Ota et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kotani et al., 2013; Nakahata et al., 2003; Ota et al., 2011).

claim: Regulation of cyclin B by PUFs is observed in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: A recent report suggests that regulation of cyclin B by PUFs is also observed in mouse embryonic stem cells (Uyhazi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Uyhazi et al., 2020).
